addressed_problems.content: Although COLT has been evaluated on ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, and Conv-3 architectures, its sparsity, stability, and transferability have not been assessed on much deeper and alternative modern architectures such as VGG16, DenseNet, and ShuffleNet. It remains an open question whether the per-iteration pruning and mask-intersection heuristic of COLT retain their advantages—fewer pruning rounds and comparable accuracy—when applied to networks with substantially more layers or different connectivity patterns (e.g., dense connections, grouped convolutions). Establishing this is essential for determining the general applicability of COLT beyond the architectures tested in this work.

The current study evaluates COLT on Cifar-10, Cifar-100, and TinyImageNet, which are relatively small-scale datasets. Whether COLT's pruning efficiency (fewer rounds) and transferability generalize to very large-scale datasets such as ImageNet and MSCOCO is unknown. Large-scale datasets introduce higher computational demands and more diverse visual patterns, which may affect the behavior of the class-based partitioning and mask intersection. Investigating this regime is necessary to assess whether COLT can be a practical pruning method for real-world large-scale applications.

COLT's pruning strategy has only been examined in the context of image classification. It is an open question whether the same cyclic overlapping lottery ticket approach can be effectively applied to other problem setups such as object detection and semantic segmentation, where output heads differ (e.g., bounding boxes, pixel-level masks), class imbalances are more pronounced, and spatial structure plays a different role. Exploring COLT-style pruning in these domains would test the generality of the hypothesis that overlapping masks from class-wise data partitions yield winning tickets, and could lead to efficient sparse models for a broader range of computer vision tasks.

The performance of COLT on compact architectures like MobileNetV2 shows slight degradation compared to LTH at high sparsities, and on ResNet-18 extreme sparsity (~97%) leads to a 5–6% absolute accuracy drop relative to the unpruned network. The causes of this degraded behavior are not yet characterized, and no mitigation strategy has been proposed. It remains an unresolved issue to systematically understand when and why COLT's aggressive pruning via mask intersection harms accuracy, and to develop modifications—such as adaptive pruning rates or alternative mask combination strategies—that preserve performance even in compact models and at very high sparsity levels.

A formal analysis of when the intersecting masks in COLT remove critical weights is lacking. While empirical evidence shows that COLT and LTH prune similar weights at high sparsities, the conditions under which the intersection discards weights that are essential for one partition but not the other are not understood. This gap hinders the development of theoretical guarantees for COLT's pruning behavior and the design of more robust mask intersection procedures. Addressing this open question would provide deeper insight into the lottery ticket phenomenon in the context of multi-partition training.

The current COLT implementation uses a fixed pruning rate p=15% and a class-based split into two partitions. It is not known how the choice of p or the number and nature of data partitions affects the trade-off between pruning speed and final accuracy. Specifically, adjusting p could influence the risk of removing critical weights, while alternative partitioning schemes (e.g., instance-based splits, more than two partitions) might yield different mask intersections. Determining optimal or adaptive strategies for setting these hyperparameters is an open problem that could improve COLT's robustness and broaden its applicability.

Neural network pruning aims to remove unnecessary parameters from overparameterized models so that a much smaller subnetwork can be trained in isolation with comparable accuracy to the original model. A prominent modern approach is the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) / Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), which identifies a binary mask $m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$ by repeatedly (i) training a full model $\mathcal{F}(x;\theta)$ to convergence, (ii) pruning the lowest-magnitude weights, and (iii) rewinding the remaining weights to their initial values. While LTH/IMP produces highly sparse “winning tickets,” it relies on many train–prune–rewind cycles: each cycle requires full training runs, producing a large computational and time cost when targeting very high sparsity. In addition, unstructured global pruning at very high sparsities risks layer collapse and may remove important weights, producing degraded accuracy. Prior transferability observations (that winning tickets found on one dataset can be reused on others) suggest potential reuse of computed masks but have not been exploited to reduce the number of IMP iterations. Thus, before this work there remained a concrete, practical gap: how to produce highly sparse, transferable winning subnetworks that (a) reach comparable accuracy to the unpruned network, (b) avoid layer collapse at high sparsity, and (c) require fewer iterative pruning rounds (and hence less training time) than standard IMP/LTH approaches.

nodes.content: In the context of magnitude-based iterative pruning, practitioners needed a concrete, operational procedure that leverages inter-partition agreement to eliminate unimportant weights more aggressively per iteration while retaining the standard IMP rewind step. Prior methods performed a single-pruning pass per iteration on the whole dataset, so reducing iteration count required a novel pruning heuristic that is (a) compatible with weight rewinding, (b) applicable with global unstructured pruning, and (c) implementable in parallel (two models trained on halves). The COLT algorithm addresses this method-design gap by specifying data partitioning, parallel training of two same-initialized models, mask creation by pruning $p\%$ low-magnitude weights per model, intersection to form $m$, and rewinding with $m$ for the next iteration.

In practice, researchers sought pruning procedures that reduce the wall-clock cost of generating winning tickets from IMP/LTH. The prior state-of-the-art IMP method required many full-training cycles: each additional pruning round implies another full training run and large latency (minutes to thousands of minutes reported). This high iteration count limited the practicality of finding highly sparse tickets for large networks and datasets. A method that reaches a target sparsity in fewer iterative train–prune–rewind cycles would directly reduce computational cost. The empirical conclusion documents that COLT resolves this performance-versus-latency gap by pruning more per iteration (via intersecting two partition-specific masks) and thereby reducing the required number of IMP cycles while maintaining final accuracy.

Generating winning tickets separately for each target dataset is costly. Prior work (Morcos et al.) observed that tickets computed on larger datasets can transfer to smaller datasets, which reduces repeated pruning costs. However, that observation had not been demonstrated for masks constructed by intersecting partition-specific tickets per iteration. The specific practical need was a pruning procedure that yields transferable masks so that one can compute a single sparse initialization on a large dataset and reuse it on smaller downstream datasets without re-running costly IMP cycles. The empirical conclusion shows COLT masks satisfy this transferability requirement and in the experiments provide equal-or-better transferred accuracy than the prior transfer baseline at high sparsities.

Global unstructured magnitude pruning can remove many weights in a single iteration, but doing so risks removing entire layer capacity (layer collapse) or deleting weights that are important under the full-data distribution. There was no simple, iterative strategy that could be more aggressive per-iteration yet maintain rewinding semantics and avoid collapse. The COLT mask-intersection heuristic targets precisely this regime: in the natural-image classification context, independent pruning on two class-wise partitions produces correlated but non-identical intermediate masks; their intersection removes weights unlikely to be critical across class splits, enabling larger effective pruning per iteration while keeping enough parameters per layer to prevent collapse. The conclusion documents that this heuristic attains that trade-off empirically and that COLT’s remaining-mask converges toward the masks LTH would select as sparsity increases.

The community required evidence about whether a new pruning heuristic would generalize across model families: shallow vs. deep, lightweight vs. full-size architectures. Prior LTH results were reported primarily for certain architectures; it was unclear whether an intersecting-mask approach would (a) preserve LTH-level performance on large/residual models, and (b) behave acceptably on compact architectures with fewer degrees of freedom. The experiments resolve this question partially: COLT attains parity or superiority for deeper/larger models and when tickets are computed on larger datasets, but its benefit is reduced or mixed for lightweight models at extreme sparsities.

A new pruning algorithm, Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT), that produces a sparse binary mask $m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$ by repeatedly performing the following operations: (1) randomly split the training class set $\mathcal{Y}$ into two disjoint halves $\mathcal{Y}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{Y}^{(2)}$ and form two datasets $D^{(1)},D^{(2)}$; (2) initialize two models with identical initial parameters $ \theta^{(1)}_0=\theta^{(2)}_0=\theta_0\sim\mathcal{D}_\theta$ and train them separately on $D^{(1)}$ and $D^{(2)}$ to obtain trained parameters $\theta^{(1)},\theta^{(2)}$; (3) for a chosen fraction $p\%$ prune the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude weights in $\theta^{(1)}$ and $\theta^{(2)}$ to obtain intermediate masks $m^{(1)}$ and $m^{(2)}$ (binary tensors with 1 = keep, 0 = prune), then form the overlapping mask $m = m^{(1)} \cap m^{(2)}$ (elementwise AND) that keeps only weight locations that both partitions agree to keep; (4) apply $m$ to rewind the remaining weights (set pruned locations to zero and reset kept locations to their initial values) and iterate the cycle. The algorithm uses global unstructured pruning and iterates until $\mathcal{F}(x; m\odot\theta)$ attains target accuracy/sparsity. The method therefore prunes twice per iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) iteration (once per partition) and advances by intersecting the two resulting masks before the next rewind.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion is a procedural description of the COLT algorithm; no empirical claim is made that could be uncertain. No load-bearing weak points or highlights were identified because the conclusion is self-validating as a defined procedure. The derivation is a specification, not a testable claim.

nodes.title: COLT: iterative pruning algorithm by intersecting masks from two class-wise data partitions

nodes.content: Empirically, the Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) algorithm produces winning tickets (sparse binary masks $m$) that achieve accuracies comparable to the unpruned network while attaining high prune rates (percentage of weights set to zero) and doing so in fewer iterative pruning rounds than the standard Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) method employing Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP). Representative results include: (a) on the TinyImageNet dataset (200 classes, 64×64 images) with a ResNet-18 architecture, the unpruned model accuracy is $72.7\%$; LTH produces an $88.8\%$-sparse ticket with $71.42\%$ accuracy in $10$ pruning rounds, whereas COLT produces an $89.1\%$-sparse ticket with $72.8\%$ accuracy in $7$ pruning rounds; (b) on TinyImageNet with ResNet-18 at extreme sparsity, the unpruned accuracy is $59.9\%$, LTH yields $97.3\%$ pruning with $53.2\%$ accuracy in $18$ pruning rounds (latency $2625$ minutes), and COLT yields $97.2\%$ pruning with $53.9\%$ accuracy in $12$ pruning rounds (latency $1756$ minutes); (c) across CIFAR-10 (10-class dataset) experiments, to reach $70\%$ sparsity COLT requires fewer rounds than LTH by 3 rounds on Conv-3 (a three-convolutional-layer plain CNN), 1 round on MobileNetV2, and 2 rounds on ResNet-18; to reach $90\%$ sparsity, COLT requires fewer rounds by 4, 2, and 3 respectively. The observed trend is that for a given target sparsity, COLT converges in fewer IMP iterations while preserving similar accuracy.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that COLT attains comparable accuracy at high sparsity with fewer pruning rounds is supported by systematic quantitative comparisons across three architectures and three datasets (H2) and by wall-clock latency measurements (H3), which establish both consistency and practical significance. However, two load-bearing uncertainties remain. P1 identifies that LTH and COLT use different per-iteration pruning rates (20% vs 15%) without control; this asymmetry is not offset by H2 or H3 because those experiments use the same asymmetric conditions, so the attribution of round reduction to the mask-intersection mechanism is partially confounded. P5 notes that all results are best-of-multiple-seeds without variance, which could inflate the advantage. The interaction: P1 threatens the quantitative magnitude of the round reduction more than its direction, and P5 adds uncertainty about stability. The highlights confirm the direction and practical relevance but do not resolve the mechanistic attribution issue. The conclusion that COLT reduces rounds is credible in direction, but the exact quantitative advantage and its causal explanation are less certain.

nodes.title: COLT attains comparable accuracy at high sparsity using fewer pruning rounds than LTH/IMP

nodes.content: Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) masks computed on a larger dataset (e.g., TinyImageNet, a 200-class dataset of 64×64 images) transfer to smaller datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, a 10-class dataset of 32×32 images; CIFAR-100, a 100-class dataset of 32×32 images) with preserved or slightly improved accuracy compared to prior cross-dataset ticket transfer results reported by Morcos et al. [22]. Quantitative transfer examples: when transferring tickets obtained on TinyImageNet to CIFAR-10, COLT achieves $90.5\%$ accuracy at $97.1\%$ prune rate versus the $89.9\%$ accuracy at $97.1\%$ prune rate reported by Morcos et al. [22]; when transferring TinyImageNet tickets to CIFAR-100, COLT achieves $65.2\%$ accuracy at $97.4\%$ prune rate versus $64.8\%$ accuracy at $97.3\%$ prune rate reported by Morcos et al. [22]. COLT consistently outperforms or matches the Morcos et al. transfer baseline at high sparsities when transferring from TinyImageNet to CIFAR datasets.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that COLT-generated tickets transfer from large to small datasets at least as well as prior methods depends entirely on an uncontrolled comparison to numbers from Morcos et al. (2019) that were not reproduced under the same pipeline (P2). Best-of-seeds reporting (P5) adds further uncertainty about the stability of the advantage. No highlight specifically underwrites the transfer comparison: H2 and H3 address round reduction, not transfer accuracy, and H1 uses transfer only as motivation for a single dataset. The primary risk (P2) is unprotected: if the Morcos numbers are not comparable, the superiority claims (0.6% on Cifar-10, 0.4% on Cifar-100) are unsupported. The conclusion that COLT transfers comparably is plausible but not independently validated within the paper, resulting in a moderate prior probability.

nodes.title: COLT-generated tickets transfer from large to smaller datasets at least as well as prior transfer methods

nodes.content: By pruning 15% of the lowest-magnitude weights independently on each of two class-wise partitions (each partition containing a non-overlapping half of the classes) derived from the same dataset and then intersecting the resulting binary masks, the Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) method removes non-overlapping low-magnitude weights more aggressively per iteration than the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) method using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), yet empirically avoids catastrophic layer collapse (the elimination of all weights in a layer). The similarity between the sets of weights pruned by COLT and LTH, defined as the fraction of identical pruned/kept parameters, is quantified: at 28% sparsity (prune rate), the similarity is about 20%; at about 48% sparsity, the similarity rises to approximately 50%; furthermore, to reach approximately 89% sparsity, LTH required three more pruning rounds than COLT in a ResNet-18 / CIFAR-100 (100-class dataset) experiment. The underlying mechanism is that intersecting masks eliminates weights that are not consistently retained by the two independent partition-trained models; because kept weights are those that survive two independent magnitude thresholds, the remaining weights are empirically robust, and the method reduces the number of iteration rounds without triggering layer collapse.

metadata.narrative: The key mechanism—that intersecting two partition-wise masks yields more aggressive per-iteration pruning—is strongly supported by the motivating experiment in H1, which shows that overlapping masks achieve 95% sparsity with only a small accuracy drop. This experiment isolates the effect of mask intersection on sparsity and provides the empirical core of the conclusion. However, two premises weaken the full conclusion. P3 identifies that the claim of avoiding layer collapse lacks formal evidence and relies only on absence of observed collapse; no layer-wise monitoring or theoretical argument is provided. P4 shows that the similarity analysis (COLT and LTH prune similar weights as sparsity grows) is based on a single run with a coarse metric, making it an unreliable sub-claim. The interaction: H1 supports the aggressive-pruning layer but does not address layer collapse or weight-similarity; P3 and P4 leave those layers exposed. The conclusion that intersection yields aggressive pruning is credible, but the sub-claims about collapse avoidance and mask convergence remain weakly supported.

nodes.title: Intersecting two partition-wise masks yields more aggressive per-iteration pruning while avoiding layer collapse; COLT and LTH prune increasingly similar weights as sparsity grows

nodes.content: Across the evaluated architectures (Conv-3, a three-convolutional-layer plain CNN with about 0.37M parameters; ResNet-18, a deep residual network with about 11M parameters; and MobileNetV2, a lightweight architecture with about 2.3M parameters) and datasets (CIFAR-10, a 10-class dataset of 32×32 images; CIFAR-100, a 100-class dataset of 32×32 images; and TinyImageNet, a 200-class dataset of 64×64 images), Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) tickets generally match or exceed Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) ticket accuracy for large/deeper architectures (ResNet-18) and for tickets computed on larger datasets; for MobileNetV2, COLT matches LTH up to moderate sparsities (e.g., ≤70%) but can underperform LTH at very high sparsities on small datasets. Observation thresholds where test accuracy drops sharply: on CIFAR-10, both methods' accuracy decreases rapidly past approximately 95% sparsity for Conv-3, 90% for MobileNetV2, and 96% for ResNet-18; on CIFAR-100, accuracy drops past 90% for Conv-3, 85% for MobileNetV2, and 95% for ResNet-18; on TinyImageNet, accuracy drops past 75% for MobileNetV2 and 85% for ResNet-18. Thus, COLT's advantages are most pronounced on larger/deeper models and when tickets are produced on larger datasets.

metadata.narrative: The conclusion that COLT's advantage is most pronounced for large/deep models and on large datasets, with mixed results for lightweight models, is supported by explicit reporting of the regimes where COLT underperforms (H4). This scope discipline strengthens the credibility of the conclusion by bounding it precisely. No load-bearing weak points specifically threaten this nuanced claim; the pattern of results (parity for ResNet-18 on all datasets, slight underperformance for MobileNetV2 on small datasets at high sparsity) is consistent across the reported experiments. The highlights confirm the honesty and specificity of the claim, making the conclusion well supported within its stated bounds.

nodes.title: COLT empirical behavior across architectures: parity with LTH for large models, mixed results for small/lightweight models

nodes.content: In the experimental comparison between the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) method using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) and the Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) method, LTH uses a per-iteration global unstructured pruning rate of 20% (0.20) of the lowest-magnitude convolutional weights, while COLT uses a per-iteration rate of 15% (0.15). This difference is stated but not controlled for; no experiment equalises the per-iteration pruning fractions across methods. The claimed reduction in pruning rounds for COLT relative to LTH is therefore not isolated from the effect of using a lower base pruning rate in COLT's per-model pruning step.

metadata.failure_mode: If the per-iteration pruning rates were equalised (e.g., both set to 20%), the observed round-reduction advantage of COLT could shrink or disappear, because COLT's per-model pruning would be more aggressive and might remove critical weights in earlier rounds, requiring additional rounds to recover. The claimed quantitative round reductions (e.g., 3–9 fewer rounds documented across datasets) would be unsupported, and the conclusion that COLT systematically reduces pruning rounds due to the overlap mechanism would be weakened or narrowed to regimes where a lower per-iteration rate is feasible.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not justify why 15% versus 20% were chosen and does not test sensitivity of the round reduction to the per-iteration rate. Since COLT's mask intersection effectively increases pruning beyond the per-model 15%, the choice of 15% may interact with the intersection effect in a way that is not separately measured. Without controlling for per-iteration pruning rate, one cannot attribute the entire round reduction to the novel mask-intersection mechanism; part may come from the different base rate or from the two-model training per round. The comparison conflates two independent design choices: the heuristic itself and the per-iteration prune fraction.

nodes.title: Unequal per-iteration pruning rates between LTH and COLT

nodes.content:
In the transfer experiment from TinyImageNet (200 classes, 64×64 images) to CIFAR-10 (10 classes, 32×32 images) on ResNet-18, the Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) method achieves 90.5% accuracy at 97.1% sparsity and is compared to the 89.9% accuracy at 97.1% sparsity reported by Morcos et al. (2019) under their own experimental setup. The Morcos et al. numbers were not reproduced under the same hyperparameters, output-layer retraining protocol, or pruning round schedule as the COLT transfer experiment; the comparison is therefore uncontrolled.Fig. 6
      Table IV
      A. S. Morcos, H. Yu, M. Paganini, and Y. Tian, "One Ticket to Win Them All: Generalizing Lottery Ticket Initializations across Datasets and Optimizers," 2019.

metadata.failure_mode: If the Morcos et al. baseline were re-produced under the identical evaluation protocol and COLT's advantage did not replicate, the conclusion that COLT transfers at least as well as prior methods would be unsupported. The specific quantitative claims of superiority (gap of 0.6% on Cifar-10 and 0.4% on Cifar-100) would lose validity, and the general claim of comparable transfer performance would reduce to an uncontrolled observation insufficient for a comparative conclusion.

refs.text: A. S. Morcos, H. Yu, M. Paganini, and Y. Tian, "One Ticket to Win Them All: Generalizing Lottery Ticket Initializations across Datasets and Optimizers," 2019.

metadata.weakness_reason: Without re-running the Morcos et al. baseline in the same pipeline, the comparison conflates differences in training protocol (learning rate schedule, weight decay, number of epochs for retraining, initialization of the new output layer) with the effect of the COLT mask itself. The reported superiority for COLT (90.5% vs 89.9% on Cifar-10, 65.2% vs 64.8% on Cifar-100) may be an artifact of these uncontrolled factors rather than a fundamental transfer advantage of COLT. The paper provides no evidence that the Morcos et al. results would hold under the exact conditions of the COLT transfer experiment.

nodes.title: Transfer baseline from literature not reproduced

nodes.content: The Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) method's mask-intersection mechanism is asserted to avoid catastrophic layer collapse (the elimination of all weights in a layer) despite pruning twice per iteration. The only supporting evidence is that no layer collapse was observed in the conducted experiments on CIFAR-10 (10-class dataset), CIFAR-100 (100-class dataset), and TinyImageNet (200-class dataset) with Conv-3 (three-convolutional-layer plain CNN), MobileNetV2, and ResNet-18 architectures. No quantitative criterion for layer collapse is defined (e.g., the fraction of remaining weights per layer below a threshold), the number of remaining weights per layer is not monitored across pruning rounds, the layer-wise sparsity distribution between COLT and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) method is not compared, and no formal proof or bound links mask intersection to collapse prevention.

metadata.failure_mode: If layer collapse were observed in a setting not tested (e.g., a deeper architecture like VGG16, a larger dataset like ImageNet, or a more aggressive per-iteration pruning fraction above 15%), the claim that COLT avoids collapse would be falsified. The conclusion that COLT achieves aggressive per-iteration pruning without triggering collapse would become unsupported outside the tested regimes, and the qualitative advantage over LTH (which also avoids collapse in those experiments) would vanish.
metadata.weakness_reason: Layer collapse is a known failure mode in unstructured global pruning where entire layers can be zeroed out, and the mitigation through conservation laws is typically shown for iterative magnitude pruning on whole datasets (Tanaka et al., 2020). The empirical observation that collapse did not occur in a few dozen runs on moderate-sized networks does not constitute evidence that the method avoids collapse in general. The mechanism of mask intersection, while plausible as a heuristic, has not been shown to satisfy any conservation-law or gradient-flow property that guarantees layer survival. The paper's reliance on absence-of-evidence as evidence-of-absence is a logical gap that weakens the claim.

nodes.title: Lack of formal evidence for layer collapse avoidance

nodes.content: The similarity analysis between Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) and Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) masks (performed on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-100, a 100-class dataset) reports one set of similarity values at five sparsity levels: 28%, 48%, approximately 57%, approximately 70%, and approximately 89%. It is not stated that multiple random seeds were used for this specific experiment. The similarity metric is defined as the number of weights pruned by both methods divided by the total number of parameters. At 28% sparsity, the similarity is about 20%, which is close to what one might expect by chance if two independent pruning criteria each prune different subsets of weights; at 48% sparsity, the similarity rises to around 50%.Fig. 7

metadata.failure_mode: If the analysis were repeated with multiple seeds and showed high variance or a flat similarity trend, the sub-claim that COLT and LTH prune increasingly similar weights as sparsity grows would be unsupported. The quantitative observations (20% at 28% sparsity, 50% at 48% sparsity) would not be reliable, and the conclusion that COLT's masks converge toward LTH's pruning decisions would be left without credible evidence.
metadata.weakness_reason: A single run without error bounds cannot indicate whether the observed similarity trend is reproducible across different weight initializations and training trajectories. Moreover, the metric definition does not distinguish between weights that become zero in both methods because they were already pruned in an earlier round, and weights that both methods newly identify as low-magnitude in the same round. The low similarity at early sparsities suggests substantial independence of the pruning decisions, which contradicts the narrative that COLT and LTH are converging to the same set of important weights and instead indicates that at early stages they prune largely different weights.

nodes.title: Similarity analysis limited in scope

nodes.content: The reported accuracy and pruning-round numbers for both the Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) method are selected as the best across multiple random seeds. The experimental procedure states that all experiments generating COLT and LTH tickets were repeated multiple times with different random initializations, and the best scores were reported. No variance, standard deviation, or range is provided for any accuracy figure or round count. This selection can inflate the apparent performance of COLT relative to LTH if one method's results have higher variance than the other's.

metadata.failure_mode: If the full distribution of results across seeds were known and showed substantial overlap between COLT and LTH in accuracy or round counts for many seeds, the conclusion that COLT attains comparable accuracy with fewer rounds would be weakened or would hold only for the best-case seed. The practical recommendation to use COLT would be less robust, and the quantitative claims (e.g., COLT needing 12 vs 18 rounds on TinyImageNet ResNet-18) would not reflect typical performance.
metadata.weakness_reason: In pruning experiments, random seed can significantly affect the final accuracy-sparsity trade-off and the number of rounds needed to reach a target sparsity. Reporting only the best seed masks the typical performance and the reliability of the round-reduction advantage. If COLT's results are noisier than LTH's (e.g., COLT has a wider spread of outcomes across seeds), the best-of-seed selection could create a spurious advantage that does not hold in the typical case. Without error bars or at least multiple-seed scatter plots, the reader cannot assess the stability or significance of the reported differences.

nodes.title: Best-of-multiple-seeds reporting without variance

nodes.content: In a preliminary experiment on Cifar-100 with an unspecified architecture (likely the same as used for Table I and Morcos et al. experiments), LTH tickets computed separately on class-wise partition 1 and partition 2 each achieve approximately 79.9% sparsity and 72.4% and 72.3% accuracy respectively when transferred to the full Cifar-100 dataset. Taking the intersection of the two partition-specific masks yields a sparsity of 95.0% while retaining 69.1% accuracy on the full dataset. This demonstrates that the overlapping mask removes additional weights that were not commonly kept by both partitions, increasing sparsity by approximately 15 percentage points with only a 3.2–3.3 percentage point accuracy drop relative to the individual partition tickets.

metadata.credit: This experiment preempts the failure mode that mask intersection would discard important weights and degrade accuracy unacceptably. It provides direct empirical evidence that the overlapping mask captures a robust core subnetwork that generalises to the full dataset: the mask prunes many weights that are not consistently important across partitions, without proportionate harm to accuracy. The quantitative trade-off (sparsity gain of 15% vs accuracy loss of about 3%) is the key empirical underpinning of the whole COLT mechanism. Without this intermediate validation, the claim that intersection is beneficial for aggressive pruning would rely solely on the final COLT results, leaving the effect of the overlap step confounded with other training choices.

nodes.title: Motivating experiment showing overlapping masks increase sparsity while preserving accuracy

nodes.content: Across three architectures (Conv-3, MobileNetV2, ResNet-18) and three datasets (Cifar-10, Cifar-100, TinyImageNet), the paper reports the number of pruning rounds required by COLT and LTH to reach target sparsities of 70%, 90%, and 98%. For example, to reach 90% sparsity on Cifar-10, COLT requires 4, 2, and 3 fewer rounds than LTH on Conv-3, MobileNetV2, and ResNet-18 respectively. On TinyImageNet with ResNet-18, COLT requires 12 rounds versus LTH's 18 rounds for approximately 97% sparsity, a reduction of 6 rounds. On Cifar-100 with ResNet-18 at 90% sparsity, COLT requires 6 fewer rounds than LTH. These comparisons are reported for all nine architecture-dataset combinations, with the exact round numbers available in the text and figures.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that round reduction is an artifact of a single dataset or architecture. By showing a consistent pattern across nine architecture-dataset combinations, the conclusion that COLT requires fewer pruning rounds is supported as a general property rather than a one-off observation. The quantitative specificity (exact round counts and differences) provides concrete, comparable evidence that allows the reader to evaluate the magnitude of the reduction across conditions. Without these systematic comparisons, the core claim would rely on a single experimental condition (e.g., Fig. 1) and would be vulnerable to confounding by dataset-specific factors or architectural peculiarities.

nodes.title: Systematic quantitative round reduction comparison across multiple architectures and datasets

nodes.content: Table IV reports wall-clock training latency in minutes for COLT and LTH on TinyImageNet with ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2 at high sparsity. For ResNet-18 at approximately 97% sparsity, LTH latency is 2625 minutes (18 pruning rounds) and COLT latency is 1756 minutes (12 rounds), a reduction of 869 minutes (33%). For MobileNetV2 at approximately 70% sparsity, LTH latency is 856 minutes (7 rounds) and COLT latency is 354 minutes (5 rounds), a reduction of 502 minutes (59%).

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode that fewer pruning rounds does not translate to practical time savings because each COLT round might be slower (two models to train, each on a half-dataset, plus mask intersection). The latency numbers directly show substantial wall-clock speedups (33–59%) for two representative high-sparsity scenarios, addressing the primary practical motivation of the paper. The quantitative magnitude strongly supports the claim that COLT reduces computational cost in real terms. Without these measured latencies, the economic benefit of fewer rounds would remain a plausible but unmeasured speculation, and the conclusion would lack practical weight.

nodes.title: Wall-clock latency reduction demonstrated

nodes.content: The paper reports that COLT's accuracy on MobileNetV2 trained on small datasets (Cifar-10, Cifar-100) slightly underperforms LTH at high sparsities, while on large models like ResNet-18 and on large datasets like TinyImageNet, COLT matches or exceeds LTH. Specifically, on Cifar-10 with MobileNetV2, both methods perform similarly up to 70% sparsity, after which COLT accuracy decreases faster than LTH. On Cifar-10 with ResNet-18, both methods drop sharply past 96% sparsity. On Cifar-100 with MobileNetV2, both drop past 85% sparsity. These breakdown points are reported per architecture and dataset in Section IV-C.

metadata.credit: This guards against the failure mode of overclaiming universal superiority. By honestly delimiting where COLT works (parity for deep/large models, on large datasets) and where it struggles (lightweight models on small datasets at high sparsity), the paper makes its conclusion about architecture-dependent behavior testable and falsifiable. This scope discipline increases the overall credibility of conclusion 5 because the evidence is presented with its limitations, not hidden. Without this explicit delineation, the conclusion that COLT is universally beneficial could be rejected by users encountering failure on MobileNetV2; with the delimitation, the conclusion remains credible within the stated regime.

nodes.title: Explicit identification of failure regimes

steps.reasoning: Define the goal and primary objects. Let $\mathcal{F}(x;\theta)$ denote a feed-forward network with parameters $\theta$. Let $\theta_0$ denote the random initial parameters drawn from an initialization distribution $\mathcal{D}_\theta$, i.e., $\theta_0 \sim \mathcal{D}_\theta$. Let $m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$ denote a binary mask where $|\theta|$ is the total number of scalar parameters; $m_i=1$ means the $i$-th parameter is kept, and $m_i=0$ means it is pruned. The objective is to compute a mask $m$ such that the pruned network $\mathcal{F}(x;m\odot\theta)$ (where $\odot$ is elementwise multiplication) achieves accuracy comparable to the unpruned network while attaining high sparsity $s\%$ and using fewer iterative pruning rounds than standard iterative magnitude pruning (IMP).

Describe the data partitioning used by the algorithm. Let $\mathcal{Y}$ be the set of class labels in the training dataset $D=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ where $y_i\in\mathcal{Y}$. Randomly split the class set $\mathcal{Y}$ into two disjoint equal halves $\mathcal{Y}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{Y}^{(2)}$ such that $\mathcal{Y}^{(1)}\cap\mathcal{Y}^{(2)}=\emptyset$. Form two class-wise datasets $D^{(1)}=\{(x_i^{(1)},y_i^{(1)})\}_{i=1}^{n^{(1)}}$ with $y_i^{(1)}\in\mathcal{Y}^{(1)}$ and $D^{(2)}=\{(x_i^{(2)},y_i^{(2)})\}_{i=1}^{n^{(2)}}$ with $y_i^{(2)}\in\mathcal{Y}^{(2)}$. The algorithm uses class-based splits (two partitions) to ensure each partition has enough instances for generalization and to increase diversity in intermediate tickets.

Specify model instantiation and independent training on partitions. Initialize two models with identical architectures and identical initial parameters: $\theta^{(1)}_0=\theta^{(2)}_0=\theta_0\sim\mathcal{D}_\theta$. Train model one on $D^{(1)}$ and model two on $D^{(2)}$ independently (parallel training is possible). After convergence, denote the trained parameters as $\theta^{(1)}$ and $\theta^{(2)}$ respectively. At the first pruning round the mask $m$ is $1^{|\theta|}$ (all ones), i.e., the models are trained unpruned for the first round; in subsequent rounds $m$ becomes sparse and is applied during training via $m\odot\theta^{(1)}$ and $m\odot\theta^{(2)}$.
Fig. 4

Define the local intermediate mask-generation operation. Let $p\%$ be the per-model fraction of parameters to prune by magnitude in a single pruning step (the authors use $p=20$ in experiments for the LTH baseline and $p=15$ for COLT in many experiments). For each trained parameter tensor $\theta^{(k)}$ with $k\in\{1,2\}$, compute an intermediate binary mask $m^{(k)}$ by setting $m^{(k)}_i=0$ for the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude parameters in $\theta^{(k)}$ and $m^{(k)}_i=1$ otherwise. This is global unstructured magnitude pruning: the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude parameters are removed across the entire set of parameters rather than per-layer.

Define the overlapping/intersection operation that produces the COLT mask. Given the two intermediate masks $m^{(1)}$ and $m^{(2)}$, compute the overlapping mask $m$ as the elementwise intersection (logical AND) of the two masks: $m = m^{(1)} \cap m^{(2)}$ which can be implemented as $m_i = m^{(1)}_i \cdot m^{(2)}_i$ for each parameter index $i$. The overlapping mask $m$ keeps only those parameter locations that both independently trained models agree to keep (i.e., locations that survive both magnitude thresholds).
Fig. 3

Describe the rewinding/pruning application step. Apply the overlapping mask $m$ to both models by performing $m\odot\theta^{(1)}$ and $m\odot\theta^{(2)}$, which sets pruned locations to zero. Then rewind the kept parameters (indices with $m_i=1$) to their initial values from $\theta_0$; concretely, for kept indices $i$ set the model parameter to $\theta_{0,i}$ and for pruned indices set to $0$. This rewind/rewriting mirrors the weight-rewinding procedure of iterative magnitude pruning methods and prepares both models for the next round of training under the same sparse mask $m$.
[21]

Describe the iterative cycle and stopping criterion. Repeat the cycle of (train on partitions with current mask $m$) $\rightarrow$ (compute $m^{(1)},m^{(2)}$ by pruning $p\%$ lowest-magnitude weights from each trained model) $\rightarrow$ (compute $m=m^{(1)}\cap m^{(2)}$) $\rightarrow$ (rewind kept weights to initialization and set pruned entries to zero). Continue iterations until the pruned network $\mathcal{F}(x;m\odot\theta)$ attains a target validation accuracy or until the desired global sparsity (prune rate) is reached. The algorithm prunes twice per IMP iteration (once per partition) and advances by intersecting the two resulting masks before the next rewind, yielding faster per-round sparsification than single-prune IMP.

State implementation choices and heuristics used in the paper. The method uses global unstructured pruning (pruning individual scalar weights across all convolutional layers), a moderate per-iteration prune fraction $p\%$ (authors use $p=15$ for COLT experiments to reduce layer-collapse risk), iterative pruning (many small prune iterations rather than one-shot), and class-wise two-partition splits (not more than two partitions to avoid too-small subsets). The final COLT ticket's output layer is replaced and reinitialized to predict all classes when evaluating on the full dataset (the output layer trained for half the classes is reinitialized to predict all classes before final evaluation). The toy example in the paper illustrates these steps numerically (initial weights, after-training weights, intermediate masks $m^{(1)}$, $m^{(2)}$, overlap $m$, and pruned weights $m\odot\theta^{(1)}$ and $m\odot\theta^{(2)}$).
Table II

Summarize the COLT algorithm as presented. The Cyclic Overlapping Lottery Ticket (COLT) algorithm therefore: (i) partitions classes into two non-overlapping halves; (ii) instantiates two models with identical initialization $\theta_0$; (iii) trains each model on its partition; (iv) prunes $p\%$ lowest-magnitude weights in each trained model to obtain $m^{(1)}$ and $m^{(2)}$; (v) intersects the masks to obtain $m=m^{(1)}\cap m^{(2)}$; (vi) rewinds kept weights to their initial values and zeros pruned weights; and (vii) repeats the cycle until target accuracy/sparsity is reached. This process prunes twice per IMP iteration and proceeds by intersecting masks before the next rewind, producing COLT masks $m\in\{0,1\}^{|\theta|}$.

Start from the established COLT procedure (conclusion 1) and the experimental setup described in the paper: experiments evaluate COLT and the LTH/IMP baseline on architectures Conv-3, MobileNetV2, and ResNet-18 trained on datasets CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet; training uses standard optimizers and iterative pruning with per-iteration global unstructured prune fractions (authors used $p=0.15$ for COLT in many experiments). These experimental details define the basis for empirical comparisons of number of pruning rounds and achieved accuracy at given sparsities.
Table III

Compare COLT and LTH on TinyImageNet with ResNet-18 using the concrete example reported in the paper. The unpruned ResNet-18 model trained on TinyImageNet achieves $72.7\%$ test accuracy when trained without pruning. Using standard LTH/IMP, the paper reports an $88.8\%$-sparse winning ticket that achieves $71.42\%$ accuracy after $10$ pruning rounds. Using COLT, the authors report an $89.1\%$-sparse ticket that achieves $72.8\%$ accuracy after $7$ pruning rounds. Thus, in this representative TinyImageNet / ResNet-18 result, COLT achieves comparable (slightly higher) accuracy at a similar high sparsity while reaching that sparsity in fewer iterative pruning rounds (7 vs. 10).
Fig. 1

Present an extreme-sparsity ResNet-18 TinyImageNet comparison from the state-of-the-art table. The paper reports (in the comparative table) that the unpruned ResNet-18 on TinyImageNet has accuracy $59.9\%$. LTH produced a $97.3\%$-pruned ticket with accuracy $53.2\%$ in $18$ pruning rounds and reported latency $2625$ minutes. COLT produced a $97.2\%$-pruned ticket with accuracy $53.9\%$ in $12$ pruning rounds and reported latency $1756$ minutes. These numbers show that at extreme sparsity COLT attains similar or slightly better accuracy while requiring fewer pruning rounds and less wall-clock latency than LTH.
Table IV

Summarize aggregate CIFAR-10 experiment comparisons across architectures. The paper reports that to reach $70\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-10, COLT required fewer IMP rounds than LTH by: 3 rounds fewer on Conv-3, 1 fewer on MobileNetV2, and 2 fewer on ResNet-18. To reach $90\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-10, COLT required fewer rounds by: 4 fewer on Conv-3, 2 fewer on MobileNetV2, and 3 fewer on ResNet-18. These per-architecture per-target-sparsity reductions in pruning rounds are reported in the CIFAR-10 results section and summarized in the text comparing COLT and LTH performance and rounds.
Fig. 5

Explain the empirical trend and mechanism that justify fewer pruning rounds. Because COLT performs pruning twice per iteration (pruning $p\%$ from each partition independently and then intersecting masks), the overlapping mask $m$ is typically sparser than a single partition’s mask and thus attains a higher cumulative prune rate per iteration compared to a single-branch IMP iteration. The experiments show that these additional per-iteration prunings do not degrade accuracy relative to LTH and therefore COLT reaches the same target sparsity with fewer iterations while preserving comparable accuracy. The authors repeat this observation across datasets and architectures in the experimental results and figures.
Fig. 3

Conclude the empirical claim. From the concrete TinyImageNet / ResNet-18 examples, the extreme-sparsity table, and the reported per-architecture CIFAR-10 summaries, the empirical observation is that COLT produces winning-ticket masks $m$ that reach accuracies comparable to the unpruned network at high sparsities and do so using fewer iterative pruning rounds than standard LTH/IMP. The paper therefore asserts that for a given target sparsity COLT converges in fewer IMP iterations while preserving similar accuracy.

Start from the COLT algorithm and the authors' transfer protocol. The paper follows the practice of transferring a computed sparse mask/ticket and its associated initialization to train on a different dataset by removing the ticket's output layer and replacing it with a randomly reinitialized fully connected layer to predict the full set of classes; to handle different input shapes the last convolutional output is globally average pooled before the new output layer. This transfer protocol defines how COLT-generated tickets computed on a large dataset can be applied to smaller datasets for evaluation.

State the relevant transferred-ticket experiments described by the authors. The authors compute COLT masks on TinyImageNet and then transfer the resulting tickets to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, comparing performance against the prior ticket-transfer baseline from Morcos et al. The transferred-ticket experiments were designed to evaluate generalization and transferability of COLT masks across datasets of the same domain (natural images).
[22]
Fig. 6

Report the quantitative TinyImageNet→CIFAR-10 transfer result. The paper reports in the comparative Table IV that when tickets are transferred from TinyImageNet to CIFAR-10, COLT achieves $90.5\%$ accuracy at $97.1\%$ pruning, whereas Morcos et al. reported $89.9\%$ accuracy at $97.1\%$ pruning. Thus, COLT transferred tickets match or slightly improve accuracy versus the Morcos et al. baseline at the same high prune rate in this example.
Table IV

Report the quantitative TinyImageNet→CIFAR-100 transfer result. The paper reports that when transferring TinyImageNet tickets to CIFAR-100, COLT achieves $65.2\%$ accuracy at $97.4\%$ pruning while Morcos et al. reported $64.8\%$ accuracy at $97.3\%$ pruning. Again, COLT's transferred ticket slightly outperforms the prior reported transfer baseline at comparable extreme sparsity.
Table IV

Summarize the empirical transfer conclusion. Combining the TinyImageNet→CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet→CIFAR-100 examples and the performance curves shown in the transfer figure, the authors observe that COLT masks computed on a larger dataset transfer to smaller datasets preserving or slightly improving accuracy compared to prior ticket-transfer results; specifically, COLT consistently outperforms or matches the Morcos et al. transfer baseline at high sparsities when transferring from TinyImageNet to the CIFAR family, demonstrating COLT's transfer capability.
Fig. 6

Treat the COLT mask-generation mechanism (conclusion 1) as established and restate the key mask operation: in each pruning round, two independent trained models (trained on class-wise partitions) produce intermediate masks $m^{(1)}$ and $m^{(2)}$ by pruning the $p\%$ lowest-magnitude weights in each model; the COLT mask is $m=m^{(1)}\cap m^{(2)}$ which keeps only parameters that both partitions agree to retain.

Explain why intersecting partition-wise masks leads to more aggressive per-iteration pruning. Pruning $p\%$ lowest-magnitude parameters independently in each partition produces two sets of low-magnitude indices; taking the intersection of the complementary keep-sets (i.e., intersecting masks) removes any weight that was pruned in either partition, so the effective fraction of parameters removed per COLT iteration can be larger than $p\%$ because a parameter pruned in one partition will be removed from the overlapping mask if it does not survive in the other partition. Thus, intersecting non-identical low-magnitude sets yields a net increase in per-iteration sparsity compared to a single-branch pruning step.

State the empirical observation that this aggressive per-iteration pruning avoids catastrophic layer collapse in the reported experiments. The authors argue and report that despite performing two pruning operations per iteration and intersecting masks (which could in principle remove many parameters and risk layer collapse), COLT empirically avoids catastrophic layer collapse because the two partition-derived tickets are strongly correlated and transferable; therefore the intersection does not systematically zero out entire layers. The authors explicitly note that tickets from partitions are correlated and that intersecting them "do not discard weights such that a complete layer gets collapsed."
[40]

Provide the quantitative similarity measurements between COLT and LTH prune choices. The paper reports a weight-similarity analysis (Fig. 7) comparing the set of pruned/kept parameters between COLT and LTH across increasing sparsities: at approximately $28\%$ sparsity the fraction of identical pruned/kept parameters between COLT and LTH is about $20\%$ (i.e., 20% of parameter locations are pruned/kept identically), and at approximately $48\%$ sparsity this similarity rises to about $50\%$. The figure also shows that at higher sparsities the two methods prune increasingly similar weights.
Fig. 7

Report the comparative pruning-round observation tied to similarity growth. Using the ResNet-18 / CIFAR-100 example shown in the figure, the authors observe that to reach approximately $89\%$ sparsity LTH required three more pruning rounds than COLT; this numerical comparison is presented alongside the similarity bars and the per-method pruning-round curves in the same figure, showing that COLT attains the sparsity earlier while LTH's pruned set gradually converges to COLT's pruned set as sparsity increases.
Fig. 7

Explain the proposed mechanism for robustness of kept weights under intersection. Because the overlapping mask keeps only weights that survive two independent magnitude-based pruning thresholds (one per partition), the remaining weights are those that are consistently high-magnitude under diverse class splits; the authors argue these weights are empirically more robust and thus removing non-overlapping low-magnitude weights via intersection reduces iteration count without triggering collapse in the reported experiments. This mechanism is asserted in the methodology and supported by the empirical observations in the weight-similarity analysis and pruning-round comparisons.
Fig. 3

Begin from the COLT procedure and the experiments comparing COLT and LTH across multiple architectures and datasets. The paper evaluates Conv-3 (a shallow 4-layer convolutional network), MobileNetV2 (a lightweight architecture with bottleneck residual blocks), and ResNet-18 (a deeper residual network) on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and TinyImageNet. The experimental protocol and architectures are described in the setup and Table III.
Table III

Report the per-architecture empirical outcomes on CIFAR-10. For CIFAR-10 experiments the paper reports: COLT and LTH perform similarly for ResNet-18 (no significant advantage for COLT); for Conv-3 the two methods perform equally; for MobileNetV2 COLT and LTH match up to moderate sparsities (up to about $70\%$ sparsity) but COLT's performance starts decreasing relative to LTH beyond that point. The authors also report pruning-breakdown sparsity thresholds where ticket accuracies for both methods drop steeply: around $95\%$ sparsity for Conv-3, $90\%$ for MobileNetV2, and $96\%$ for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10.
Fig. 5

Report per-architecture observations on CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet and summarize mixed behavior. For CIFAR-100 the paper reports COLT and LTH behave similarly up to moderate prune rates for ResNet-18 and in some regimes COLT outperforms LTH after $80\%$ pruning; for MobileNetV2 and Conv-3 the two methods are almost similar with LTH slightly better at some prune rates. For TinyImageNet the two methods again perform similarly for most sparsities, with COLT slightly better than LTH at some levels. The authors note that MobileNetV2 tickets sometimes underperform COLT on small datasets but match when trained on larger datasets like TinyImageNet and when transferred. Overall, the results indicate that COLT advantages are pronounced for larger/deeper architectures and for tickets computed on larger datasets.
Fig. 5

State the paper's synthesis concerning architecture and dataset scale. The authors conclude that COLT tickets generally match or exceed LTH ticket accuracy for large/deeper architectures (ResNet-18) and for tickets computed on larger datasets (e.g., TinyImageNet). For MobileNetV2 (a lightweight architecture) COLT matches LTH up to moderate sparsities (e.g., $\leq 70\%$) but can underperform LTH at very high sparsities on small datasets (CIFAR-10 / CIFAR-100). For very shallow networks (Conv-3) the two methods perform similarly. Thus, COLT's advantages are most pronounced on larger/deeper models and when tickets are produced on larger datasets.
Fig. 5

Conclude with the reported sparsity-breakdown thresholds and the overall empirical message. The paper reports specific sparsity thresholds at which ticket accuracies drop sharply across datasets and architectures (CIFAR-10 drop points: Conv-3 ~95%, MobileNetV2 ~90%, ResNet-18 ~96%; similar dataset- and architecture-dependent breakdowns are reported for CIFAR-100 and TinyImageNet). From these results the authors infer that COLT provides parity with LTH for large models and mixed results for small/lightweight models, with the strongest COLT benefits appearing for deeper architectures and tickets generated on larger datasets.

open_questions.content: The paper explicitly identifies several unresolved directions and limitations for future study: (1) Evaluate COLT’s sparsity, stability, and transferability on much deeper and other modern architectures (examples mentioned: VGG16, DenseNet, ShuffleNet) and on very large-scale datasets (examples mentioned: ImageNet, MSCOCO) to determine whether the per-iteration pruning and mask-intersection heuristic retain their advantages beyond the evaluated regimes. (2) Explore COLT-style pruning in other problem setups such as object detection and semantic segmentation where output heads, class imbalances, and spatial structure differ from image classification. (3) Further characterize and mitigate the observed degraded behavior in compact architectures (e.g., MobileNetV2) and at extreme sparsities (reported example: $\sim$97% pruning yields 5–6% absolute accuracy drop on some ResNet-18 experiments), including formal analysis of when intersecting masks may remove critical weights and how to tune $p\%$ or partitioning to prevent such losses. These items are presented as explicit future-work limitations and experimental regimes to be investigated.
